description: Firefix brings together four Computer Science students and one International Relations & Law student to combat extreme wildfires. Risk management requires historical baselines, yet the gap between MODIS (2000) and higher-resolution VIIRS (2012) sensors distorts long-term trends. With Sutellite, we harmonize over 25 years of NASA thermal records into an intuitive, accessible visual platform to spot seasonal fire patterns and critical anomalies at a glance.
summary: Sutellite is a climate intelligence and risk management platform that transforms over 231 million official NASA active-fire observations into clear, comparable, and actionable insights. As extreme wildfires escalate globally, emergency managers, environmental agencies, and insurers need decades of historical baselines to assess risk; however, technical differences between NASA’s MODIS sensors (1 km nominal resolution, operational since 2000) and VIIRS sensors (375 m resolution, operational since 2012) prevent direct dataset merging without distorting long-term trends. To solve this, we built a real data engineering pipeline that standardizes official records from both sensors into a canonical 35-field Parquet schema over a 0.1° spatial grid, achieving rigorous structural harmonization while preserving scientific differences. Built upon this validated foundation—while also allowing users to upload their own UTF-8 CSV or Parquet files—Sutellite integrates a descriptive statistical engine with CSV exports, a dual anomaly-detection system powered by an Isolation Forest machine learning model cross-checked with MODIS burned-area data, and an interactive web dashboard featuring KPIs, 3D/2.5D global visualization, and dedicated accessibility modes for colorblindness and dyslexia.
details:
The Real-World Problem We Solve

The unprecedented rise of extreme wildfires demands data-driven prevention and risk assessment. While NASA provides over two decades of open active-fire records through MODIS (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21), both systems differ significantly in spatial resolution (1 km vs. 375 m), detection sensitivity, confidence scales, and file schemas. Merging these datasets directly creates artificial spikes and distorts historical trends. Moreover, hundreds of millions of raw satellite detections are inaccessible to local authorities, forestry managers, and analysts lacking big-data infrastructure.

Market Opportunities, Target & Viability

Raw NASA archives require heavy data engineering to harmonize, while private geospatial consultancies act as costly "black boxes." Sutellite bridges this gap as an open, transparent intelligence layer for three core targets:

  • Insurers (B2B): Recalibrate risk models on a standardized 0.1° grid and validate claims via Fire Radiative Power (FRP).
  • Public Agencies & Civil Protection (B2G): Prioritize prevention budgets and receive automated anomaly alerts without big-data teams.
  • Agroforestry & Energy (B2B): Monitor asset exposure and comply with anti-deforestation laws (e.g., EUDR) by uploading custom CSV/Parquet files.

Freemium Business Model: Free open access to the global atlas and CSV exports for researchers and public transparency, paired with Pro SaaS & API subscriptions for enterprises and agencies needing automated AI alerts, unlimited custom uploads, and direct Parquet API feeds.

How It Works: System Architecture in 4 Modules

1. Data Engineering & Structural Harmonization Pipeline (MODIS + VIIRS)

  • Official Data Ingestion & Canonical Schema: We collected official active-fire observations from NASA FIRMS (separating historical ARCHIVE records from Near Real-Time NRT data) across eight critical study regions: Angola, Australia, Brazil, California, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Indonesia, Spain, and Zambia. We designed a standardized 35-field canonical schema (coordinates in EPSG:4326, timestamps in UTC, and Fire Radiative Power FRP), while preserving sensor-specific attributes such as original confidence systems.
  • Processing & Integrity Validation: Using a Python data engineering pipeline, we transformed raw CSV files into Parquet format with automated schema checks, manifests, and checksums. During validation, we processed 64 Parquet files totaling ~231.36 million observations with zero schema inconsistencies (retaining 20 records with negative FRP values and flagging them via quality flags rather than altering original measurements).
  • Spatial-Temporal Aggregation & Custom Uploads: Focusing on 2013–2025 for cross-sensor comparison, we divided regions into a common 0.1° spatial grid aggregated by month and grid cell. This achieves structural harmonization—allowing side-by-side comparison of detection counts and FRP statistics while keeping individual satellite platforms identifiable—without falsely claiming physical equivalence or treating missing detections as confirmed zeros. Users can also upload their own UTF-8 CSV or Parquet files (up to 25 MiB) to generate instant spatial summaries and seasonal comparisons.

2. Descriptive Analytics & Statistical Engine

  • Built on top of the harmonized datasets, the platform computes multi-year baselines, seasonal curves, land-cover fire shares, and intensity distributions (detection counts, mean/total FRP, and historical medians).
  • Users can dynamically filter by region, year, sensor (MODIS or VIIRS), and individual satellite (Terra, Aqua, Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21), and download filtered statistical tables directly in CSV format.

3. Dual Anomaly Detection & Isolation Forest AI In many regions, seasonal agricultural burning occurs every year; the critical operational challenge is distinguishing normal seasonal fire activity from severe, atypical outbreaks. Sutellite addresses this through two complementary analytical views across 0.1° grid cells compared against the exact same calendar month in previous years:

  • Historical Comparison (2000–2025): Evaluates a selected month against prior years with comparable records (requiring at least three historical years). Early records from MODIS Terra/Aqua are regionally calibrated onto the VIIRS S-NPP scale using the 2013–2022 overlap period while preserving estimation bounds; a cell is flagged only when the lowest current estimate exceeds the highest historical upper bound.
  • AI Anomaly Detection (2024–2025): Analyzes VIIRS detections against a fixed 2013–2023 reference baseline using an Isolation Forest machine learning model. The algorithm evaluates both raw hotspot counts and how sharply they deviate from the historical monthly average for that specific cell. An AI alert is triggered only when two strict criteria are met simultaneously: the Isolation Forest model classifies the activity as statistically anomalous and the count exceeds the historical maximum recorded during the 2013–2023 baseline. Clicking any alert cross-references ESA WorldCover 2021 land-cover classes and verifies whether MODIS MCD64A1 mapped physical burned area in that cell.
  • Real-World Validation Example: In Angola (August 2025), a single 0.1° grid cell recorded 12 active-fire detections compared to a historical upper limit of just 1 detection across five prior Augusts. Both the historical comparison and the Isolation Forest AI flagged the cell as a severe anomaly, which was independently confirmed by MODIS burned-area data mapping ~174 hectares of burned land in that exact cell and month.

4. Interactive Dashboard, KPIs, 3D/2.5D Globe & Accessibility

  • Interactive Atlas & KPIs: Integrates key performance indicators (KPIs), monthly trend charts, interactive timelines, night mode, and multilingual support (English, Spanish, and Basque).
  • 3D / 2.5D Globe & Multi-Layer Maps: Users can explore the globe in interactive 3D or 2.5D perspective to select regions and inspect multi-layer maps filtered by land cover type, FRP intensity, or hotspot detection counts.
  • Inclusive Accessibility: Features dedicated UI modes including a Colorblind mode (high-contrast palettes, symbols, and values across maps and charts) and a Dyslexia mode (clean typography with increased CSS letter-spacing, word spacing, and line height to prevent character crowding).

Team Lineup

  • Ainhoa — Data Engineering & Satellite Harmonization (Computer Science): Leads the data processing pipelines (Parquet and CSV), cleaning, structuring, and harmonizing NASA FIRMS records from 2000 to the present to reconcile resolution and sensitivity differences between MODIS and VIIRS sensors.
  • Ane — Data Science & Statistical Modeling (Computer Science): Develops the statistical engine and historical metrics from the harmonized datasets, building multi-year baselines and the Global Burning Activity Calendar to enable unbiased risk analysis.
  • Alena — Artificial Intelligence & Anomaly Detection (Computer Science): Designs and implements the machine learning models (Isolation Forest and cross-sensor historical anomaly detection) responsible for identifying atypical patterns and early thermal alerts.
  • Ainare — UI/UX Design & Interactive Visualization (Computer Science): Crafts the web interface, accessibility modes, and visual experience of the platform, turning millions of satellite detections into dynamic 3D/2.5D maps and clear visual calendars.
  • Selene — Business Strategy, Regulatory Framework & Communications (International Relations & Law): Defines the business model, regulatory alignment, and commercial viability of the project, while leading the narrative and executive pitch to connect our technology with emergency managers, insurers, and public agencies.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

We utilized Artificial Intelligence at two distinct levels in Sutellite:

  • Core Platform Machine Learning: We implemented an Isolation Forest anomaly-detection model trained on historical cell-level monthly time series (2013–2023 reference baseline) to automatically identify unusual surges in active-fire hotspot counts and severity during 2024–2025.
  • Development Assistance Tools: We used GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, and Claude to accelerate boilerplate coding, optimize Python data-processing queries within our Parquet pipeline, debug frontend visualization components, and refine technical documentation. All code, statistical algorithms, and scientific outputs were manually verified and validated by our team. No AI tools were used to generate official NASA logos or insignias.
dataRefs: NASA Earthdata – MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer): Official historical and recent active-fire detections (Terra and Aqua satellites, 2000–present) and MODIS MCD64A1 monthly burned-area validation data.
NASA Earthdata – VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite): Official 375 m high-resolution active-fire detections from Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21 satellites (2012–present).
NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System): Historical ARCHIVE and Near Real-Time NRT active-fire datasets used to build our 35-field canonical schema.
NASA GIBS (Global Imagery Browse Services) & NASA Earth Observatory: Satellite imagery tile services and reference map base layers integrated into the platform's spatial viewer.
projectRefs: ESA WorldCover 2021 v200 (European Space Agency): Global 10 m land-cover classification (Copernicus Sentinel data, CC BY 4.0) used to contextualize fire detections and AI alerts across dominant terrain classes (grassland, tree cover, cropland, shrubland, built-up, and bare land).
Natural Earth: Public-domain vector and raster basemap datasets used for rendering administrative boundaries and geographic context across the 3D/2.5D globe and regional views.
